sections.COMMENTS:
The Northern Apennines Arc represents the interface between the Apennines chain in the upper plate and the Adria lithosphere in the lower plate.
ITSD002 puts in contact the Umbria-Marche Meso-Cenozoic units over the Adriatic foreland (Lavecchia et al., 2003, 2007); in its easternmost part, ITSD002 represents the detachment level in common among the thrust ramps currently active in the Adriatic offshore and in the Po Plain.
This regional discontinuity is well imaged in the CROP03 seismic reflection profile (Barchi et al., 1998; Finetti et al., 2001; Lavecchia et al., 2004), and has been interpreted: 1) as a major lithospheric structure, cutting the whole crust from the metamorphic basement up to the shallower levels (Barchi et al., 1998; Lavecchia et al., 2003, 2004); or 2) as one of the leading elements of the accretionary prism of the Apennine belt (Bally et al. 1986; Doglioni et al. 1994). In the latter case the earthquakes are thought to occur at the interface where the sedimentary cover is delaminated from the metamorphic basement.
This shallower part of ITSD002 is imaged by geological and seismic reflection cross sections (Barchi et al., 1998; Fantoni and Franciosi, 2010; Artoni 2013; Turrini et al., 2015, 2016; Bonini, 2018; Livani et al., 2018) and is characterized by a low-angle detachment at the base of the Mesozoic succession or, in the outer front of the Po Plain, within the Miocene succession.
Some authors (Bally et al., 1986; Doglioni et al., 1994) indicate the bottom of the Triassic evaporites as the basal decollement level and propose that thin-skinned tectonics has characterized the Paleogene-Neogene evolution of the belt. Other investigators (Barchi et al., 1998; Finetti et al., 2001; Lavecchia et al., 2003) consider that also the upper portion of the magnetic basement was involved in thrusting and propose a thick-skinned structural style. In general, there is a good agreement among the researchers (e.g.: Barchi et al., 1998; Calamita et al., 1994; Coward et al., 1999) about the presence of two main decollement levels inside the accretionary prism, the lower one coinciding with the bottom of the Triassic evaporites, on which the major thrust ramps originate, and the shallower one coinciding with the Marne a Fucoidi or Scaglia Cinerea formation, on which minor thrusts sheet detach.
The lateral variation of the dip of the Northern Apennines Arc interface may have been controlled by inherited discontinuities in the lower plate (Vannoli et al., 2015) that likely also governed the shape of the frontal thrust arcs in the Po Plain (Livani et al., 2018) and the regional change in the shape of the foredeep from cilindrical to non-cilindrical (Amadori et al., 2019). Among others, Vannoli et al. (2015) maintain that the thrust belt shows undulations controlled by inherited Mesozoic horsts and grabens, with recesses unfolding around horsts and salients developed upon grabens (Cuffaro et al., 2010).
The intermediate-to-deep earthquakes distribution, Moho position from receiver function and mantle anisotropy below the Northern Apennines Arc all concur to suggest a complex process of crustal delamination and sinking of the Adria continental lithosphere (Giacomuzzi et al., 2012; Chiarabba et al., 2014, 2015; Piana Agostinetti and Faccenna, 2018). This process is laterally discontinuous with an abrupt interruption south of the 43Â° parallel, where intermediate-to-deep instrumental seismicity is virtually absent and the Adria lithosphere appears flat (Chiarabba et al., 2015). Variations in seismicity and upper mantle structure indicate a change in tectonic processes from delamination retreat in the central Apennines to crustal under-plating in the northern Apennines (Chiarabba et al., 2014).
The long-term shortening rate across the Northern Apennines Arc is in the order of 2.9 mm/yr during the entire development of the orogeny (Basili and Barba, 2007). Present-day regional geodetic estimates (Bennet et al., 2012), numerical modeling (Carafa et al., 2015; Pezzo et al., 2020), and further syntheses (Panara et al., 2021) indicate rates of activity along the Apennines front in the 0.6-2.5 mm/yr range.
From a seismotectonic point of view, the geometry of the interface represented by ITSD002 is intended to capture both the earthquakes associated with the interface itself and the earthquakes located within the crustal thickness of the lower plate below, for whom it is not possible to define the geometry of a seismogenic fault.
Based on regional seismological and geophysical data, we deem that the 12-20 km depth range on this Source is the one at which most seismic moment release is occurring.
Historical and instrumental earthquakes that can be associated with the activity of the Northern Apennines Arc are: 14 September 2003 Appennino Bolognese (Mw 5.2), 23 December 2008 Parmense (Mw 5.4), 24 April 1741 Fabrianese (Mw 6.2), 12 March 1873 Appennino Marchigiano (Mw 5.9) (Rovida et al., 2021).
The macroseismic fields of these earthquakes are characterized by wide felt areas, which suggest rather deep hypocenters, indicating potential seismic release on deeper structures (Sbarra et al., 2019).
Other seismic events, like the 26 March 2008 Lunigiana (Mw 4.2) and the 27 January 2012 Appennino Parmense (Mw 5) ones, show instrumental depth (72 km) suggesting a location within the lower plate. One further event, the 25 October 1972 Appennino Settentrionale (Mw 4.9), shows an expected hypocentral depth (45 km), compatible with an intra-slab fault (Sbarra et al., 2019).

pictures.c: Depth distribution of deep crustal and subcrustal earthquakes and geometry of the Adria lithosphere flexured beneath the Apennines. The lowermost profile cuts across the Marche region (from Chiarabba et al. [2005]).

pictures.t: Map of depth of seismogenic layer in Italy
pictures.c: A map of the depth of the bottom of the seismogenic layer in the Marche region shows progressively deeper earthquakes moving westward from the axis of the Northern Apennines. Shallower depths are again found along the Adriatic coastline (from Chiarabba et al. [2005]).

The Stress Map of Italy shows a NE-SW compressional tectonic regime acting in the coastal Marche region. The directions of Shmin follow the trend of the Northern Apennines fronts from the southern Marche to the Po Plain (from Montone et al. [2004], modified).

pictures.t: Profile of seismic activity in the Northern Marche
pictures.c: The profile highlights the earthquake activity of the central-northern Apennines along the Coastal Thrust Front (CTF) and the occurrence of a strip of deeper events to the southwest, possibly related to the deeper portion of the same thrust (from Burrato et al. [2004]).

The easternmost lithospheric thrust according to Barchi et al. [1998]. It is assumed that the upper crustal seismicity occurring between 14 and 20 km falls on this thrust. This model assumes a thick-skinned tectonic context. From Barchi et al. [1998], modified.

Present activity of the Apennines belt front in the Adriatic region according to Carminati et al. [2004]. It is assumed that the deeper seismicity of the Marche region occurs at the base of the accretionary prism near the interface between the slab and the sedimentary cover.

pictures.t: Distribution of deep earthquakes in the Northern Apennines
pictures.c: Synthesis of existing seismic data in the northern Apennines: epicentral distribution and focal mechanism of deep earthquakes (from Lavecchia et al. [2003]).
Lithospheric thrusts according to Lavecchia et al. [2003]. The Adriatic Thrust is the active and seismogenic structure in this model of thick-skinned tectonics.

pictures.t: Seismogenic and mechanical zoning of the Adriatic Thrust (sensu Lavecchia)
pictures.c: The depth of the seismogenic layer varies from the internal to the external sector of the Apennines. Notice that the hypocentral depths follow the geometry of the thrust, increasing from the coastal zone to the western sector (from Lavecchia et al. [2003]).

pictures.t: Regional cross-sections across the Po Plain and the northern Adriatic Sea
pictures.c: Interpreted regional seismic reflection profiles straddling the full extents of the Adriatic basin, including the Po Plain and the adjacent Northern Apennines (to the west), Southern Alps (to the north), and Dinarides (to the east) (from Fantoni and Franciosi [2009]).
